data.title: 10 best personal loans in Singapore with lowest interest rates (Nov 2026)
data.description:
If you're in urgent need of money, but are too paiseh to borrow from your family and friends, your best bet is probably a personal loan.

With a personal loan, you borrow cash from a bank or financial institution and pay them back in fixed instalments over an agreed period. But you'd typically need to meet a couple of eligibility requirements before you get it approved. Stuff like your income and credit history.

In this article, I'll break down the key terms you'll come across frequently while browsing loan listings-plus highlight the best personal loans in Singapore .

Psst… I'm also going to let you know about the great promotions you can capitalise on if you apply for some of these personal loans with MoneySmart. So keep reading!

Note: Interest rates are approximate and may vary based on individual credit profiles and prevailing market conditions. Please consult the respective banks for the most accurate and up-to-date information.

1. At a glance: Best personal loans in Singapore (Nov 2026)

Here are the current starting personal loan interest rates on offer from the most popular providers in Singapore. We'll use the example of a Singapore citizen earning $3,500 a month, who wants to borrow $10,000 and repay it over 3 years.

2. Hold up. What do interest rate, EIR and processing fees mean?

There's quite a bit of jargon here, so let's go through some points of confusion that may be swimming around in your head.

Interest rates

Notice that interest rates are quoted as “from X%” instead of being stated simply as “X%”? That’s because personal loans are pretty dynamic as they all depend on factors such as your credit history and the loan amount.

EIR

EIR stands for Effective Interest Rate. Taking into consideration other fees (like processing fee; see next point) and the loan repayment schedule, it is a more accurate reflection of the cost of borrowing than the advertised interest rates.

Processing fees

This is the main hidden cost of personal loans and is worth highlighting. The processing fee is deducted from the principal—meaning, for a $10,000 loan with a $100 (or 1%) processing fee, you get only $9,900 in cash. As a borrower, you might not “feel” it, but it does eat into your funds and increase the cost of borrowing.

Now, let's walk through the 10 featured personal loan packages.

3. DBS Personal Loan

The DBS personal loan is only open to existing customers. If you already have (1) a DBS Cashline account or have a DBS credit card and (2) credit your salary into a DBS deposit account, you can get the cash disbursed instantly.

The loan is open to Singaporeans and PRs, as well as foreigners with DBS Cashline or credit card accounts. You must be aged 21 to 70 years with a minimum annual income of $20,000-this opens up DBS personal loans to include slightly older groups of people and lower income earners compared to other banks.

Like the Standard Chartered CashOne loan, you don't need to earn a regular salary to be eligible for this loan. Self-employed individuals and commission earners can also apply.

DBS's personal loan promises interest rates as low as 1.48 per cent. There is a processing fee of 1 per cent, bringing the lowest possible EIR to 3.22 per cent. Loan tenures of 6 months to 5 years are available.

Do note that these are the lowest possible rates and the actual interest rate depends on what DBS is prepared to extend to you.

4. Trust Instant Loan

When they say "instant", they mean it. Trust's personal loan, called Trust Instant Loan, disburses cash to you in just 60 seconds with the Trust credit card.

This is how it works: You have a Trust credit card with a certain available credit balance at any one point in time. The Trust Instant Loan converts a portion of that balance into cash for you. Spend that cash on anything you want!

The Trust Instant Loan is open to all Trust customers. Given how it works, as I just explained above, you do need to have a Trust credit card to be eligible. But this isn't a bad thing-for one thing, it makes repaying the loan seamless. Each month, you'll see your loan instalment charged to your credit card bill. To pay the instalment, simply pay through your credit card statement via your Trust App.

The Trust Instant Loan is also EXTRA affordable with an interest rate starting from just 1.00 per cent p.a. (EIR from 2.28 per cent p.a.). They also charge no processing fees, annual fees, or the like. However, there is a three per cent early repayment fee on your remaining loan amount if you repay the rest of your loan early.

The Trust Instant Loan is open to Singapore Citizens, PRs, and Foreigners aged 21 to 65 years old. You could be a salaried worker, commission-based, or self-employed as long as your annual income is $30,000 for Singaporeans or $60,000 for Foreigners.

5. CIMB Personal Loan

The CIMB Personal Loan is another personal loan that comes with no processing fees. Its interest rate currently starts from 0.89 per cent p.a. (EIR from 1.72 per cent p.a.). This is because of an ongoing 11.11 promotion (till Nov 18). You're essentially getting a 0.11 per cent interest rebate when you apply for a loan in this period. Make sure it has a tenure of between 12 to 60 months.

You also get flexible loan tenure options of 12, 24, 36, 48 or 60 months.

For shorter loan tenures of three or six months, you could also get 0 per cent interest. But that does come with a one-time processing fee of 0.99 per cent (EIR of 5.99 per cent p.a.).

As far as eligibility goes, the CIMB Personal Loan is fairly standard. It's open to Singapore Citizens and Singapore PRs with a minimum annual income of $20,000, and to Malaysians earning at least $30,000 a year.

You'll also need to be 21 to 70 years old-that maximum age sits between the Citibank and DBS personal loan age limit. There's no prerequisite to have a CIMB Bank Account or CIMB credit card before you apply, so go ahead as long as you meet the criteria above.

Like any personal loan, you'll incur a penalty fee if you try to repay it early. For the CIMB Personal Loan, this fee is three per cent of the outstanding loan amount or $250, whichever is higher.

6. UOB Personal Loan

UOB's personal loan is only open to existing UOB credit cardholders or CashPlus customers who are Singaporeans, PRs aged 21 to 65. You'll also need to be a salaried worker earning at least $30,000 a year. Not an existing UOB customer? You'll have to get a UOB credit card or CashPlus to apply for a UOB Personal Loan.

The interest rate is from 1.00 per cent p.a. for loan periods of 12, 24, 36, 48 or 60 months, with a 1.93 per cent p.a. EIR.

While UOB used to only waive processing fees for loan periods 24 months and up, processing fees are now waived for all loan periods.

If you're an existing UOB customer, you can get instant approval when you apply for your personal loan online.

7. Standard Chartered CashOne

Standard Chartered CashOne personal loan is open to Singapore Citizens, PRs and foreigners with a Singapore Employment Pass aged 21 and above.

The barriers to entry for the Standard Chartered CashOne personal loan have gone up slightly. The minimum annual income requirements are now $30,000 for Singaporeans and PRs and $90,000 for foreigners. You also don't necessarily need to be a salaried worker to apply-Standard Chartered is cool with salaried employees, variable/commission-based employees, and even self-employed individuals.

You can apply for this personal loan online by signing in through Singpass and receive your loan disbursement within 15 minutes-it's super easy. There's no need to be an existing Standard Chartered customer to get this personal loan.

So, it's fast-but is it also affordable? Standard Chartered charges an initial annual fee of $199 (deducted from your approved loan) for any loan tenure between one to five years. From the second year onwards, you won't have to pay any more annual fees — unless you miss any instalments, in which case you will pay $50 in annual fees for that year. 

Plus the late payment fee of $100. If you pay your full monthly instalment on time for the first six months, you won't have to worry about late penalties. After that, you'll have the flexibility to pay just the minimum-whichever is lower: $50 or one per cent of your approved monthly principal.

So taking the $199 annual fee into consideration, I'd say CashOne is more worthwhile if you're taking out a big loan.

Interest rates are advertised as starting from 0.90 per cent, working out to an EIR of 1.75 per cent and above. In reality, interest rates are personalised, so yours might differ from this example.

8. HSBC Personal Loan

HSBC's personal loan is open to Singaporeans and PRs aged 21 to 65 years old with an annual income of $30,000 and above for salaried workers, and $40,000 for self-employed or commission-based workers. Foreigners must earn at least $60,000 a year and have an employment pass with at least six months' validity.

The best part about HSBC's personal loan is its long loan tenure of up to seven years — currently the longest loan tenure in Singapore. So if you need to borrow a large sum but can't afford high monthly repayments, HSBC's personal loan is definitely one you should consider.

HSBC has dropped their promotional interest rates even further now starting from 1.30 per cent p.a. with an EIR from 2.50 per cent p.a. with no processing fees. Remember, however, that actual interest rates will vary from person to person.

Another factor to consider is that HSBC's personal loan comes with an annual fee of $120, and only the first year's fee is waived. Don't miss your payments, or you'll be subject to a $120 late payment fee.

9. GXS FlexiLoan

GXS is a digital bank that's 60 per cent owned by Grab and 40 per cent owned by Singtel. Now, don't be dissuaded by the idea of a digital bank. Like any regular bank, GXS offers customers a personal loan-and a decent one at that.

With a loan tenure between two and 60 months, GXS FlexiLoan instalment plan interest rates could start from as low as 1.00 per cent p.a.. However, do note that you'll only receive this advertised rate if you name your loan "MSDEAL". Another caveat here is that this lower rate will be awarded as cashback. Meaning to say actual advertised rates hover at around 2.88 per cent p.a. (EIR from 5.45 per cent p.a.).

On top of all that, GXS FlexiLoan doesn't charge any annual, processing, early repayment or late fees-something almost unheard of when it comes to loans from your traditional banks. You heard that right, repay your loan early with no extra charges! However, GXS will charge you late interest if your repayments are late, so you won't get off scot-free.

One downside to the GXS FlexiLoan is that foreigners aren't eligible. It's only for Singapore Citizens and Singapore Permanent Residents between 21 and 65 years old. The minimum annual income is $20,000.

10. MariBank Instant Loan

The MariBank Instant Loan is a fully digital personal loan that focuses on speed and simplicity. It offers a starting interest rate of 1.28 per cent p.a. with an EIR from 1.92 per cent p.a., and there are no processing fees, which helps keep borrowing costs down.

You can choose loan tenures ranging from three to 60 months, and once approved, funds are typically disbursed almost instantly. While the loan is tied to a Mari Credit Card, you don't need to be an existing cardholder-one will be issued automatically upon approval.

Eligibility is limited to Singapore Citizens and PRs aged 21 and above with a minimum annual income of S$30,000. Applications are done entirely via the MariBank app, using Singpass.

Do note that early repayment incurs a fee of three per cent of the outstanding amount or S$100 (whichever is higher), and missed payments may attract high credit card interest charges, so this loan is best for borrowers who can commit to regular repayments.

11. Citibank Quick Cash with Ready Credit (New Customers)

I'm going to preface this by saying that the 3.45 per cent (EIR from 6.50 per cent) interest rate for the Citi Quick Cash personal loan is only available to customers who are completely new to Citibank loans. If you already have a Citibank loan, you'll be given a higher interest rate.

The plus point for this one is definitely the ease of getting your funds. You'll be easily able to convert the credit balance on your Citi Credit Card or Citibank Ready Credit account into cash. Just log into the Citi Mobile App, key in the amount of cash you need and you can get the funds pretty much instantly.

Citi Quick Cash is open to Singapore Citizens and PRs (salaried or self-employed) with a minimum annual income of $30,000, and foreigners with an annual income of at least $42,000. The eligible age range is 21 to 65 years.

With Citibank's Quick Cash personal loan, you can choose a tenure of 12, 24, 36, 48, or 60 months-all with zero processing fees. You'll get a 3.56 per cent interest rate on Citibank's personal loan with a shorter 1-year tenure, or 3.45 per cent if you intend to extend your loan repayment to three years. While the interest rates differ according to tenure period, you'll get an EIR of 6.5 per cent for all.

That said, don't take our word for it. Rates are customised, so its best to enquire with the bank directly.

12. OCBC ExtraCash Personal Loan

While the OCBC ExtraCash Personal Loan has the highest interest rates (from 5.43 per cent p.a. / EIR from 11.47 per cent p.a.) on this list, it does come with some perks that might make it a solid choice for some. If you need a large loan, you can borrow up to six times your monthly income, with fixed repayments spread over 12 to 60 months.

Like many of the other loans mentioned, it offers fast disbursement when you sign up via Myinfo. Plus, it has a relatively low entry requirement — just $20,000 in annual income for Singaporeans and PRs. You'll also be able to easily see a full breakdown of all your outstanding payments via internet banking.

However, punctual repayments are a must. A late payment will set you back $80, and if you decide to restructure or repay early, you'll be charged a three per cent fee on your outstanding balance. So, be sure of your loan tenure before committing!

13. Which personal loan should you choose?

Cheapest personal loans in Singapore

- Standard Chartered CashOne Personal Loan
- UOB Personal Loan
- CIMB Personal Loan
- Trust Instant Loan
 

Personal loans with fastest disbursement

- GXS FlexiLoan

- DBS Personal Loan
- Trust Instant Loan

- HSBC personal loan

Personal loan with longest repayment tenure

- HSBC personal loan

Personal loans to consider if you want to take a huge amount

- Standard Chartered CashOne Personal Loan
- OCBC ExtraCash Personal Loan 

Whatever personal loan package you choose, opt for the smallest loan amount and shortest term you can comfortably manage. This will keep your interest payments to a minimum.

Remember that the actual interest rate a bank offers you will depend on factors like your credit history, how much you want to borrow and for how long. So if you don't get offered the lowest advertised interest rates with one bank, it's worth comparing what other banks can offer to find the cheapest personal loan for your profile.

There are certain groups of individuals that may have a harder time taking out a personal loan.

Older individuals: If you're above 65 years old, DBS/POSB and CIMB will let you apply for personal loans up to the age of 70 years.

Those earning an annual income below $30,000: Most of the loans I've listed above have a minimum requirement of about $20,000 annual income, so you have plenty of options if this pertains to you.

Commission-based workers or self-employed individuals: Citibank Quick Cash, HSBC Personal Loan, DBS Personal Loan and Standard Chartered CashOne are good options. Some other banks may only accept salaried workers.

14. Term loan vs credit line-which should you choose?

While researching personal loans, you might have come across many different loan types, some of which do not seem to fit what we described above.

We usually recommend these loans because they have much lower interest rates. You can pay back slowly and steadily at a pace comfortable to your financial situation.

Many banks also offer a personal line of credit-sometimes called a credit line, revolving loan, or even "flexible repayment loan".

This is a pre-approved amount of money you can cash out in part or whole, but you need to repay it ASAP or else face sky-high interest rates. Don't fall for it unless you're absolutely confident you can pay the money back immediately.

These days, most banks base their personal loans on either your personal line of credit or credit card limit. So you will need either a credit card or credit line to get the loan. However, it is still considered a term loan if it comes with a structured repayment plan.

But before you sign up, understand that your credit cards with this bank will be as good as dead because you'll have effectively "spent" your credit on a cash loan.

15. Being in debt is not fun…

But it can be prevented. If you must take out a loan, channel all your energies into paying it off on time to avoid late charges. In the meantime, re-examine your income and budget, making a note of everything you spend on, so you won't have to resort to loans again.

Ideally, you should draw up a budget that gives you enough leeway to set aside some cash for the future without starving to death.

You should also build up an emergency fund worth a few months' expenses. If you're hit with unforeseen circumstances, you can dip into this fund instead of having to take a loan.

It's also a good idea to know what types of insurance you need. We recommend hospitalisation insurance at a bare minimum, and life insurance if you have dependents. Being sufficiently insured ensures that you don't get hit with huge bills if the unexpected happens.

This article was first published in MoneySmart.

data.title: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year as tech sell-off worsens
data.description:
NEW YORK - A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday (Nov 20) pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7 per cent, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.

The benchmark S&P 500 index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10 per cent from its Oct 6 all-time high.

The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.

The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3 per cent, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9 per cent.

Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 8.5 per cent.

The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each fell more than 5 per cent overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.

AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.

The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks' big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data centre construction winning at both the federal and state level.

"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over."

Much of the AI rout was centred among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centres. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3 per cent, Micron Technology slid 13.9 per cent and Broadcom fell 12.2 per cent. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7 per cent.

Corning slid 10.9 per cent and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3 per cent.

Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 14 per cent lower. The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 30 per cent.

The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 8.5 per cent to $88.91 (S$114.69), but remains above its IPO price of US$83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing US$2 trillion in value.

Anthropic's share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23 per cent decline from its brief peak of US$115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.

Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50 per cent in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.

Outside of tech, several companies managed to gain ground despite strong downward pressure on the market. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7 per cent and homebuilder Lennar gained 1 per cent.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.

While the stock market's mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.

The University of Michigan's latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists' expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the US war with Iran.

Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93 per cent from 5.04 per cent late Thursday.

Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6 per cent to settle at US$92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the US war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.

Source: Associated Press

data.title: Democrats open probe into Nvidia influence on US Megaspeed investigation
data.description:
NEW YORK — Democratic lawmakers have opened a probe into what influence Nvidia was able to wield over a US Commerce Department investigation of cloud company Megaspeed for possible illegal diversion of chips to China, according to a letter reviewed by Reuters.

In the November 19 letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, the House Democrats said they wanted to know "whether the department allowed a major American corporation that is financially and personally linked to the Trump administration to interfere with enforcement activity."

Singapore-based Megaspeed has attracted public attention since news broke that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of being a Chinese spy. Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday. China has denied Alice Huang is a spy.

Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner that operates data centres, has been under US investigation for two years, the departments of Commerce and Justice said this week. They said Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia in May 2025 about sales to the company and, with Singaporean authorities, conducted an on-site inspection in June 2025 at Megaspeed and interviewed Alice Huang.

In August 2025, Nvidia contacted Commerce employees directly and requested a meeting with one of them, a Commerce official told Reuters, referring to the investigators. Nvidia told them Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler said the company could communicate with the employees.

"The American public and Congress deserve a full accounting of what happened, " US Representatives Gregory Meeks, ranking member of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California wrote in the letter, which requested answers and relevant documents by December 1.

"BIS conducts all enforcement strictly by the book," a spokesperson for the department's Bureau of Industry and Security said in a statement. "BIS enforces aggressively across the board, including with respect to chip smuggling."

Megaspeed said it complies with all applicable laws, including US export control requirements.

An Nvidia spokesperson said that, as an American company it consults with department officials to answer questions, provide information and request their guidance and instructions.

"We look forward to engaging with Congress on this matter," the statement said.

Source: Reuters

data.title: Alibaba defrauded shareholders by concealing ties to suspected spy in Nvidia scandal, lawsuit says
data.description:
NEW YORK — Alibaba was sued on Thursday (Nov 19) in New York by shareholders who accused the Chinese e-commerce giant of defrauding them by concealing its ties to the suspected Chinese spy whose relationship with former Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang contributed to his resignation last week.

According to a proposed class action filed in Manhattan federal court, Alibaba inflated its share price by knowingly and materially understating in its 2024, 2025 and 2026 annual reports the risks that actual or suspected export control violations could harm its business.

Shareholders cited Alibaba's relationship with Megaspeed, a ​Singaporean company suspected of helping Beijing gain access to advanced Nvidia AI chips, and whose executive Alice Huang had a relationship with Jensen Huang, who is not related to her.

The shareholders said Alibaba shares fell 14 per cent over four days last week because of media reports on Alibaba's ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, including that Alibaba had become Megaspeed's "dominant" customer.

They attributed part of the decline to a Nov 12 Reuters article that said Nvidia's spy scandal could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on Chinese AI companies' remote use of ‌advanced processors.

Alibaba did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Eddie Wu, its chief executive, is also a defendant.

Nvidia itself faces several shareholder lawsuits over the spy scandal, including allegations of lax oversight by its directors.

Wu said on Thursday that Alibaba remained on track for US$100 billion (S$128 billion) in external cloud revenue and a 20 per cent EBITDA margin by 2030, despite US curbs on access to computing power that could affect the company's products and services next year. The restrictions were imposed after Huang resigned from Nvidia.

In June, Alibaba sued the US government over being added to a blacklist of "Chinese military companies" that the Department of Defence linked to that country's military.

Last month, a federal judge in California granted Alibaba an injunction barring the US government from denying Pentagon ​contracts to companies whose lobbyists also work with designated Chinese military companies.

Alibaba said that restriction caused its lobbyists to retreat because they feared losing other clients, and violated its First Amendment constitutional right to speak to and petition the government.

Thursday's lawsuit by Alibaba shareholder Withida Bihan seeks unspecified damages for holders of Alibaba's American depositary shares between May 23, 2024 and Nov 11, 2026.

Source: Reuters

data.title: Asian shares head for worst week since 2020 as AI rout deepens
data.description:
HONG KONG/SINGAPORE — Asian shares fell on Friday (Nov 20) , heading for their worst week since 2020, as Anthropic's debut failed to restore investor faith in the AI sector, while the dollar extended a rally on safe-haven flows.

MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan lost 3.2 per cent, its biggest single-day drop in over a month. The gauge has now sunk 8.3 per cent this week, its worst performance since March 2020.

Japan's Nikkei tumbled 4.1 per cent and was headed for a 6.8 per cent weekly drop, while South Korea's KOSPI fell 4.4 per cent and was set to end the week 7.1 per cent lower. Taiwan shares were down five per cent on Friday and 16 per cent for the week, their biggest weekly decline since 1991.

The moves in Asia followed losses of more than two per cent for the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite after Anthropic, the world's first publicly traded frontier AI company, saw its shares surge in a historic debut but the euphoria failed to lift other stocks.

"Risk aversion intensified as investors continued to unwind crowded positioning and reassess the broader macro backdrop following Anthropic's record-shattering IPO," said Preston Pagli, markets analyst at Citi.

He added that Nvidia's blowout earnings earlier in the week failed to become the reset markets had hoped for, while sentiment deteriorated further after Anthropic's IPO failed to spark a broader rally.

Further adding to the unease, a report on AMD from a media outlet associated with short-selling fund Hunterbrook Capital raised concerns that the chipmaker's ties to Chinese entities, some linked to blacklisted firms, could draw greater US regulatory scrutiny to the sector.

The AI trade has already been battered by Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, growing momentum for the anti-data-centre movement following Democrats' sweep of the US midterm elections, and concerns over the sector's rising debt loads.

"No one headline drove the roll though some pointed to an AMD short report which tapered overall sentiment. Overall, it just felt like more questions than answers out there today with most wondering what gets this tape to feel better?" said Goldman Sachs analysts in a trading note.

They said asset managers and hedge funds net-sold macro products while they net-bought pockets of consumer and financials, with liquidity remaining poor, which is exacerbating price action.

US stock futures also pointed to further losses, with the S&P 500 futures down 0.2 per cent and Nasdaq futures down 0.6 per cent in Asia on Friday.

Dollar extends rally, treasury yields dip on risk aversion

As risk sentiment took a beating, the US dollar extended its rally on safe-haven bids, while also being supported by growing expectations of a more hawkish Federal Reserve.

Fed funds futures imply that a quarter-point rate hike next month is essentially locked in, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.

The dollar index last traded steady at 103.86, after rising to its highest since April 2025 this week, and is now on track to post its fourth week of gains.

In government debt, US Treasury yields eased as the sharp equity selloff pushed investors toward safe-haven bonds. The yield on benchmark 10-year Treasury notes held steady at 5.02 per cent, near a one-week low. The two-year yield touched 4.749 per cent, compared with a US close of 4.779 per cent.

Oil prices were mostly steady after an earlier spike, as reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz offset pressure from rising US crude inventories and forecasts for a global oil surplus.

Brent crude futures rose 0.4 per cent to US$92.37 (S$120) a barrel but remained on track for a third week of declines.

Non-interest-bearing gold slid 2.5 per cent to US$3,533.40 an ounce and was headed for a nine per cent weekly loss.

data.title: TSMC tightens China AI chip curbs as new US rules close manufacturing loophole, sources say
data.description:
Taiwan's TSMC is tightening restrictions on Chinese chip designers, suspending some previously permitted advanced manufacturing orders and generally limiting affected customers to older chipmaking technology, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The move could close one of the last remaining routes for Chinese companies to produce powerful AI processors, complicating Beijing's efforts to develop domestic alternatives to chips designed by Nvidia and manufactured by TSMC.

The world's largest contract chipmaker has instructed that affected orders using manufacturing processes of 16 nanometres and below be halted unless customers obtain US export licences, the people said.

Chinese designers will generally be limited to older 28-nanometre and 40-nanometre processes, provided their chips do not use high-bandwidth memory (HBM) or require advanced packaging, according to TSMC guidance reviewed by the two people.

Most leading AI chips are produced using seven-nanometre processes or smaller, enabling faster and more energy-efficient performance. HBM allows processors to handle the vast data volumes required by AI applications, while advanced packaging integrates chips and memory to boost computing power.

US closes manufacturing route

The restrictions follow new US Commerce Department rules that took effect on Thursday, removing a compliance route that had allowed some Chinese designers to access advanced manufacturing services without individual export licences.

Previously, TSMC could check the computing power and other technical characteristics of certain Chinese chip designs to determine whether they fell outside US export controls.

Under the new rules, TSMC can no longer use that verification process for affected Chinese customers. Their advanced chips are instead presumed to be covered by US controls, requiring export licences unless an exception applies.

The Financial Times first reported on Thursday (Nov 19)  that TSMC and South Korea's Samsung Electronics had suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers following the new restrictions.

China's AI chip ambitions

The measures could particularly affect Chinese companies developing alternatives to Nvidia's processors, including independent chip designers and technology giants that have developed in-house chips.

A US government list of approved chip designers includes Nvidia, AMD, Apple and Taiwanese companies MediaTek and Realtek, but no mainland Chinese firms.

Some Chinese AI chip designers still had access to TSMC's seven-nanometre manufacturing technology before Thursday, a separate source with direct knowledge of the matter said. Reuters could not independently verify the arrangements under which those chips were manufactured.

TSMC's guidance also requires closer scrutiny of customers' operating locations, parent companies, major shareholders, packaging providers and shipping routes, the people said.

The checks extend to orders placed through overseas subsidiaries or intermediaries, including entities in Taiwan, the US, Europe, Japan and Southeast Asia.

Source: Reuters

data.title: Oil prices edge higher as Houthi attacks on Riyadh raise supply concerns
data.description:
TOKYO — Oil prices edged higher on Friday (Nov 20), though set for a weekly decline, as concerns over supply disruptions grew following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude futures rose 24 cents, or 0.3 per cent, to US$92.22 (S$120) a barrel by 1.18am GMT (9.18 am SGT). US West Texas Intermediate futures for December climbed 19 cents, or 0.2 per cent, to US$83.40 a barrel, while the more-active January contract gained 20 cents, or 0.2 per cent, to US$82.64.

Both benchmarks settled little changed on Thursday but Brent is set for a 3.5 per cent decline for the week while the December WTI contract is set for a six per cent weekly drop as expectations of a supply surplus grew because crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels. Brent and WTI are set to fall for the third week in a row.

"Concerns over Middle Eastern crude oil supplies have resurfaced due to attacks on Riyadh by the Houthis, prompting buying," said Satoru Yoshida, a commodity analyst with Rakuten Securities.

"Expectations that coordinated production cuts will continue at the OPEC+ meeting later this month are also providing support," he said.

The Iran-aligned Houthi movement fired missiles at Riyadh, the latest blow to the kingdom in its war with the Houthis.

Two oil tankers also hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and "exploded" and "are burning", Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a statement carried by state media on Thursday.

OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on Nov 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The group comprises the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia.

The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4 per cent by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday.

In Russia, crude oil output could fall again as Ukrainian attacks on refineries and export infrastructure intensify, analysts and traders say. Ukrainian drone attacks have slashed Russian oil refineries' combined crude processing volumes by 45 per cent since late October, Reuters reported on Wednesday.

Separately on Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that Moscow would hit back hard after Ukraine struck the bridge linking Russia and Crimea for a third time this week and said he was dropping any idea of a moratorium on attacking energy sectors and shipping.

Source: Reuters

data.title: Trump bought up to $323k of Nvidia stock in September, disclosure shows
data.description:
WASHINGTON — US President Donald Trump bought as much as US$265,000 (S$323,000) in Nvidia stock and sold as much as US$15,000 worth of the stock ​in September, weeks before reports surfaced of CEO Jensen Huang's ties to an alleged Chinese spy, according to Trump's latest financial disclosure released on Thursday (Nov 19).

US lawmakers have been asking questions about Trump's knowledge of Huang's personal life, and the president has said he "was amazed" by the allegations against Huang, who is among the president's closest allies in Silicon Valley.

Trump administration officials are currently weighing policies ⁠that could shape Nvidia's future, including rules governing exports of ​its advanced chips. Nvidia faces heightened scrutiny after news reports surfaced that Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman accused of spying for Beijing. Reuters has not independently confirmed that the woman is a spy.

The Nvidia ⁠trades were among hundreds the president made in September, according to the disclosure signed ​by Trump on November 1 and made ​public by the US Office of Government Ethics ⁠on Thursday. In August, Trump bought as much as US$1.6 million worth of Nvidia shares and sold as much as US$1 million worth, Reuters previously reported.

Trump also bought as much as US$315,000 in SpaceX stock in September, according to the same disclosure. SpaceX is a US ​military contractor run by Trump's former adviser Elon Musk. 

The company has billions of dollars' worth of contracts with the US government, and its fortunes are often tied to approvals from federal agencies. Trump has traded SpaceX stock over the course of his second term as president, including in June and July 2026.

Reuters could not immediately determine the precise amount of Trump's trades because federal officials use ranges to declare the value of their assets on their financial disclosure forms.

Trump's portfolio managed separately: White House

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement that third-party financial institutions independently manage the president's portfolio and replicate "recognised indexes, such as the Schwab 1000".

"Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold," Ingle said.

Nvidia is the world's leading maker of advanced AI chips, widely used to develop cutting-edge AI systems. The US has for years sought to limit China's access to Nvidia's most advanced chips, driven by concerns that China could use them to build weapons or superior AI tools.

Nvidia executives, including Huang, have argued for broader access to China. Chinese companies and researchers have also repeatedly found ways around the US export restrictions.

On Monday, the Trump administration said it would further limit China's access to advanced AI chips from companies such as ​Nvidia by restricting shipments of advanced chips to Southeast Asian countries, which Chinese companies have used to access computing power to train AI models.

The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed in 2025 on Huang's relationship with the woman and on intelligence that she was giving information to the Chinese government, ​and that he chose not to act on ​the findings. Questioned about the New York Times reporting, Trump said he "was amazed" by the allegations against Huang.

data.title: Esso drops fuel prices for first time since Sept 14
data.description:
Chandra Asri-owned Esso has become the latest major fuel company here to drop fuel prices.

In a price board update posted on Thursday (Nov 19) evening, Esso announced that it has reduced prices across its 92-, 95- and 98-octane petrol grades, as well as diesel.

The 3-cent per litre reduction mirrored the same drop posted by Caltex on Nov 4, and Shell and Sinopec on Nov 18.

SPC is the only major fuel company here that has not adjusted prices this week.

However, the PetroChina-owned company was also the only retailer that did not join in the last round of price hikes recorded between Oct 29 and Nov 2.

Instead, SPC's last posted price adjustments were on Oct 16.

Following the latest reduction by Esso, the price of the more popular 95-octane petrol at major fuel companies now ranges from $3.56 at SPC to $3.60 at Caltex, Esso, Shell and Sinopec.

Meanwhile, Union Gas-owned Cnergy and Smart Energy are offering the petrol grade at $2.74 and $2.62 respectively.

Oil prices rose on Thursday following losses in the prior session as worries about Middle East supplies amid attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz pushed up against expectations for a market surplus.

At 10.16pm, Brent crude futures were trading at US$1.24, or 1.35 per cent a barrel. 

Meanwhile, US West Texas Intermediate futures for December climbed $1.29 or 1.6 per cent to US$84.55.

The December contract expires on Friday.

During a trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, Trump said he and Xi felt strongly about oil having to flow through the Strait of Hormuz.

Still, risks remained for Middle East oil supply amid renewed hostilities in the region.

On Nov 18, Iran said it targeted US drone and missile sites in Kuwait overnight after the United States struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, marking Tehran's first attack on the US-allied Gulf state since September.

The next day, on Nov 19, Riyadh's tallest skyscraper, headquarters of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, was struck by a suspected Houthi missile in the latest blow in the Iran-backed Yemeni group's war with the kingdom.

data.title: Stocks fall as Anthropic debut fails to ease AI concerns; dollar rises
data.description:
NEW YORK/LONDON — Global stocks fell on Thursday (Nov 19) with sliding tech shares as Anthropic's debut failed to allay investor concerns about AI returns, while oil prices rose as attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz grabbed market attention.

Investors have said that Anthropic's market reception over the coming days and weeks will be heavily scrutinized to gauge broader sentiment toward investments in artificial intelligence. The Claude developer's initial public offering was priced at US$83 (S$107) a share, valuing Anthropic at about US$1.5 trillion before the stock rose as much as 39 per cent to trade at US$115.10.

"Investors are making changes in their portfolio to incorporate Anthropic, so I wouldn't extrapolate a whole lot of meaning from (Thursday's) trading behaviour, whether it's up or down," said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital in St. Louis.

Ellerbroek pointed to a leadership change in chipmaker Nvidia and to shrinking bets on the growth in data centre capex as having an impact on investors.

"Data centres are going to be more expensive to build and they're going to be built more slowly," Ellerbroek said.

Anthropic's stock closed up 17 per cent on its debut, valuing the company at just below US$1.8 trillion.

"We can't underestimate the importance of this IPO. It sort of serves as a valuation for the wider AI ecosystem," said Fiona Cincotta, senior market analyst at StoneX.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,101.11 points, or 2.19 per cent, to 49,097.06, the S&P 500 fell 147.80 points, or 2.02 per cent, to 7,175.83 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 550.68 points, or 2.25 per cent, to 23,879.20.

MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe fell 17.76 points, or 1.65 per cent, to 1,056.80. The pan-European STOXX 600 index fell 0.88 per cent, while emerging market stocks fell 18.79 points, or 1.27 per cent, to 1,465.49.

 Dollar and oil edge higher

The dollar ticked up against developed peers but some sensitive currencies sold off on concerns about tightening financial conditions. Mexico's peso fell 1.4 per cent and Colombia's peso dropped 1.8 per cent.

"We're seeing a scramble for US dollar liquidity, and the entire emerging market complex is suffering a severe selloff as global financial conditions tighten," said Karl Schamotta, chief market strategist at Corpay.

"With sentiment on the US technology sector showing signs of crumbling while expectations for the Fed's policy path climb, stress is rising in the currencies most exposed to a slowdown in the AI buildout," Schamotta said.

Against a basket of peers, the greenback has climbed to 19-month highs on the back of expectations of tighter monetary policy out of Washington. On Thursday, the dollar index rose for an eighth consecutive session and was up 0.14 per cent to 103.96.

In commodities, oil prices settled flat on the day but were higher late as earlier reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz more than offset rising US crude inventories and forecasts for a global oil surplus.

Iran's navy said in a statement carried by state media that two oil tankers hit naval mines in the waterway and "exploded" on Thursday. Reuters could not independently verify the report.

US crude rose 0.66 per cent to US$83.81 a barrel and Brent rose to US$92.72 per barrel, up 0.84 per cent on the day.

Spot gold fell 2.54 per cent to US$3,627.55 an ounce, and spot silver fell 4.36 per cent to US$43.04 an ounce. Copper declined 0.14 per cent to US$12,453.00 a ton.

Source: Reuters
